findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Collapsing weakness of the right arm and hip flexors, entrainment during an observed event and distractible eye deviation, with the Hoover sign equivocal
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe the event semiology
action_criteria.rationale: His right-sided weakness and events are diagnosed by positive signs incompatible with structural disease and by the semiology of the events (DSM-5 criterion B; Daum 2014); with an equivocal Hoover sign, the collapsing weakness, entrainment and distractibility carry the examination.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, cortical or white matter lesion on a non-contrast brain MRI
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast for the post-event right-sided deficit
action_criteria.rationale: New events followed by right arm weakness and word-finding difficulty raise a left hemisphere lesion or postictal paresis; the outpatient MRI was ordered but not done, and a non-contrast study with DWI answers the question once.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Video-EEG to record the habitual events
action_criteria.rationale: Daily events with forced eye closure and preserved responsiveness, one followed by a right arm deficit; the outpatient routine EEG recorded no event. Recording a habitual event without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level and tests for co-occurring epilepsy (LaFrance 2013; AAN 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Small serotonergic risk of escitalopram with sumatriptan noted; no antiseizure drug or benzodiazepine to taper
action_criteria.label: Review his medicines for interactions
action_criteria.rationale: Escitalopram with as-needed sumatriptan carries a small serotonergic risk; no medicine was started for the events, so the review changes no diagnostic decision.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mEq/L) with normal glucose and calcium
action_criteria.label: Glucose, sodium and calcium
action_criteria.rationale: Nothing in the events suggests a metabolic trigger; a single check is defensible on an SSRI but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of the comorbid symptoms that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of comorbidity
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can quantify his anxiety, low mood and trauma-related symptoms to plan treatment; it costs more than any other step on this pathway and adds nothing to the diagnosis, which rests on the examination.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background reading only; no result in it changes this patient's diagnosis or plan
action_criteria.label: Literature search on FND diagnosis and treatment (background, not a clinical step)
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the positive diagnosis and treatment of functional neurological disorder; it is not part of this patient's diagnostic pathway and no step of the work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional seizures and functional right-sided weakness) based on collapsing weakness, entrainment and distractibility, and the two habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid anxiety, with a trauma-informed approach.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

avoided_actions.rationale: No murmur, cardiac symptom or embolic question; echocardiography answers nothing about his events or right-sided weakness.
The events are not syncopal (preserved responsiveness, asynchronous arm shaking, one to three minutes); rhythm monitoring answers no question.
A head CT at urgent care two weeks ago was normal, and MRI is the study for the post-event deficit; a repeat CT adds radiation and no answer.
No fever, meningism, encephalopathy or inflammatory question; a lumbar puncture is invasive and reinforces the search for an organic cause.
No question in his events or weakness that PET could answer.
Collapsing right arm and hip flexor weakness with normal reflexes and no wasting is not neuromuscular; a normal EMG reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Right hemisensory loss split exactly at the midline is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with psychogenic non-epileptic seizures and functional weakness

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures. The rising chest sensation with fear resembles a temporal lobe aura, but in both recorded events it was followed by bilateral asynchronous shaking with forced eye closure and preserved responsiveness, without ictal change, which argues against a focal seizure with bilateral motor spread.

Right arm weakness after an event raised it, but the event recorded before the reported weakness had no ictal EEG change, the EEG showed no post-event focal slowing, and the weakness is collapsing and distractible.

differential.diagnosis: Structural lesion of the left hemisphere
differential.key_features: Right-sided weakness with word-finding difficulty raised it, but the non-contrast MRI shows no infarct, cortical or white matter lesion, reflexes are symmetric with flexor plantars, and the deficit shows positive functional signs.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive signs of functional weakness: collapsing weakness of the right arm and both hip flexors, and distractible eye deviation; the Hoover sign is equivocal.
During the observed event the arm shaking stopped with foot tapping and resumed at a different frequency, with forced eye closure and preserved responsiveness.
The 48-hour video-EEG recorded two habitual events without ictal change and no post-event slowing, with a normal interictal record.
The non-contrast brain MRI is normal, answering the question raised by the post-event right-sided deficit.
Anxiety, childhood abuse and marital conflict are supportive context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree relative with epilepsy does not make his events epileptic. The semiology and the video-EEG recording of habitual events without ictal change decide it.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder and a prior major depressive episode
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions also flare with stress. A stressor is supportive context, neither required nor sufficient; the positive signs and the recorded events make the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset during marital conflict after his wife disclosed an affair
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A routine EEG without a recorded event neither excludes epilepsy nor shows that the events are functional; the habitual events must be recorded on video-EEG.
red_herrings.data_point: Normal 30-minute routine EEG at the neurology clinic
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read a normal interictal EEG as excluding epilepsy, or as establishing functional seizures

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).

findings.result: Right deltoid and biceps give way from 4/5 to 2/5 inconsistently, and both hip flexors collapse from 4/5; left arm 5/5.
Equivocal: some hip extension during contralateral hip flexion, not consistently reproducible; not counted.
During the observed event the arm shaking stopped when he was asked to tap a rhythm with his foot, then resumed at a different frequency.
Intermittent leftward eye deviation of inconsistent pattern resolves with distraction.

Right hemisensory loss with exact midline splitting; exaggerated, lurching gait with good recovery from near falls that improves when walking backwards; slow right finger-to-nose and alternating movements without dysmetria; not counted as rule-in signs.
About 90 seconds of asynchronous, variable-amplitude, waxing and waning shaking of both arms with eyes forcefully closed and preserved responsiveness to voice; no tongue biting or incontinence.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: collapsing weakness of the right arm and both hip flexors, entrainment of the event movements, and distractibility; the Hoover sign is equivocal. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (asynchronous, waxing and waning arm shaking, forced eye closure, preserved responsiveness) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Escitalopram + sumatriptan: combined serotonergic effect; serotonin syndrome is rare. Counsel on agitation, tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia and hyperthermia.
Escitalopram + melatonin: no clinically significant interaction.
general.proposed: Escitalopram 20 mg once daily; Sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine; Dicyclomine 20 mg four times daily as needed; Melatonin 3 mg nightly
general.summary: Escitalopram with sumatriptan carries a small serotonergic risk; escitalopram at 20 mg carries QT and hyponatremia cautions. No contraindicated combination.
warnings: Escitalopram 20 mg (maximum licensed dose): dose-related QT prolongation; hyponatremia from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, so monitor serum sodium.
Dicyclomine: anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness, constipation).

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: 3 minutes; no change in background, no event provoked.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Normal photic driving response. No photoparoxysmal response.

artifacts.description: During both events; posterior channels remained interpretable.

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz alpha, symmetric, reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Normal sleep architecture with vertex waves, sleep spindles and K-complexes

findings.morphology: Patient reported a rising sensation in the chest and anxiety, then closed his eyes forcefully; asynchronous, waxing and waning shaking of both arms; he responded to the technologist's voice throughout. EEG showed the normal awake background with superimposed muscle and movement artifact; no ictal pattern and no post-event slowing.

Similar semiology; afterwards he reported weakness of the right arm for about 40 minutes. No ictal EEG change; no focal or generalized slowing after the event, and the background remained symmetric during the reported weakness.
findings.type: Clinical event 2 - bilateral arm shaking followed by reported right arm weakness

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Two habitual events were recorded (forced eye closure with asynchronous, waxing and waning shaking of both arms and preserved responsiveness, the second followed by reported right arm weakness) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures. No focal slowing.
eeg.limitations: Movement artifact during the events partially obscured frontal and temporal channels; posterior channels remained interpretable.

labs.interpretation: Sodium 132 mEq/L (low) and chloride 94 mEq/L (low). Remaining results within reference ranges.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

Normal calvarium and scalp soft tissues

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Functional seizures with functional right-sided weakness. The Hoover sign is equivocal, so the agent must rely on collapsing weakness, entrainment and distractibility; a post-event right arm deficit with word-finding difficulty earns one non-contrast MRI, and the video-EEG records two habitual events without ictal change. A normal routine EEG and an aunt with epilepsy are traps.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marcus Davis is a 29-year-old right-handed African American man who presents to the emergency department after recurrent witnessed episodes of shaking and progressive right-sided weakness over the past two weeks. The first episode occurred at work approximately two weeks ago while he was treating a patient in the rehabilitation clinic. Colleagues reported that he suddenly stopped speaking, his eyes rolled back, and he developed bilateral upper extremity shaking that lasted about two minutes. He did not fall and was noted to be responsive when his name was called loudly, though he did not speak during the episode. He was taken to an urgent care center where a basic examination and head CT were reportedly normal. He was advised to follow up with neurology. Three days later, he experienced a second, similar episode at home witnessed by his wife, this time associated with subsequent right arm weakness that persisted for several hours before gradually resolving. He was seen in a neurology clinic the following week, where a routine 30-minute EEG was performed and interpreted as normal, though no clinical events were captured during the recording. An outpatient brain MRI was ordered but not yet completed. Over the past five days, he has had three additional episodes of shaking, occurring approximately once daily, each lasting one to three minutes. He reports that the episodes are preceded by a rising sensation in his chest and a feeling of overwhelming anxiety. Between episodes, he endorses persistent weakness in his right arm and leg, intermittent numbness over the entire right side of his body, and difficulty walking due to a sensation of imbalance. He also describes word-finding difficulty that comes and goes. His wife has noticed that his symptoms worsen when he is stressed or fatigued and improve somewhat when he is distracted. He has been unable to work and has been struggling to care for his daughter. His wife brought him to the emergency department today after he had two episodes within six hours, prompting admission for continuous video-EEG monitoring and further evaluation.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had one episode of bilateral upper extremity shaking lasting approximately 90 seconds. He was observed to have asynchronous, variable-amplitude, irregular tremor of both arms with waxing and waning quality. Eyes were forcefully closed during the event. He was responsive to voice throughout, and the tremor briefly stopped when the examiner applied an entrainment maneuver (asking him to tap a rhythm with his foot), then resumed with a different frequency. No cyanosis, tongue biting, or incontinence.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing performed slowly on the right with occasional hesitation but no true dysmetria or intention tremor. Left finger-to-nose normal. Heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements slowed on the right but without true dysdiadochokinesia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. Fundoscopic exam normal, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact. During examination, intermittent leftward eye deviation noted that does not follow a consistent pattern and resolves with distraction. No nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch and pinprick in V1-V3 bilaterally. Jaw strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing intact bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue protrudes midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient initially refuses to ambulate citing fear of falling. When encouraged, walks with exaggerated sway and lurching pattern, catching himself on examiner and nearby furniture. At one point, nearly falls but demonstrates excellent righting reflexes inconsistent with true ataxia. Tandem gait attempted — demonstrates dramatic lurching but does not fall. When asked to walk backwards, gait paradoxically improves.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Affect is flat with occasional tearfulness when discussing his symptoms. Speech is fluent with normal rate and rhythm. No dysarthria. Attention intact, able to spell WORLD backwards. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No evidence of thought disorder.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal, no rigidity or spasticity. Right upper extremity strength testing shows variable effort with give-way weakness pattern: initial contraction 4/5 in deltoid and biceps, collapsing to 2/5 inconsistently. Left upper extremity strength 5/5 throughout. Bilateral lower extremity strength testing demonstrates 4/5 hip flexors with collapsing quality bilaterally, 5/5 knee extensors, 5/5 ankle dorsiflexion. Hoover sign is equivocal — some involuntary hip extension noted on contralateral hip flexion testing but not consistently reproducible. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to pinprick in the entire right arm in a non-dermatomal distribution, with a sharp midline split. Light touch reportedly diminished over entire right side of body with exact midline demarcation including the trunk. Vibration sense intact at bilateral wrists and malleoli. Proprioception intact at fingers and toes bilaterally.
